question: European farmers are having to endure, on the one hand, the financial burden of achieving the climate targets to which the EU has committed itself (involving cutting emissions, water and soil consumption, thus reducing the agricultural output) and, on the other hand, the pressure from rising production costs, unfair competition from imports from non-EU countries, red tape, pest infestations and a drop in agricultural subsidies.

This is a direct call on the Commission to defend the food production sector, which has always been considered strategic for the social and economic viability of the EU, and to respond to the hundreds of thousands of farmers protesting in various Member States.

To avoid the gradual impoverishment of European farmers, which in the medium term would lead to a slump in production, an increase in dependence on raw food materials from abroad and the loss of the high quality and safety standards which the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy has ensured for decades, can the Commission say what concrete measures it intends to take to alleviate the costs of the energy transition and emissions reduction in the agricultural sector?
answer: The new Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) provides support to farmers for energy transition and climate action. It contributes to the Union’s environmental and climate commitments, including targets for 2030 as set out in the Farm to Fork Strategy (1) and the EU Biodiversity Strategy (2), together with other EU and national instruments.

Ring-fencing for climate, environment and animal welfare under each CAP Strategic Plan (CSP) of at least 25% of direct payments for eco-schemes and at least 35% of European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development spending, contribute to reaching those targets. Actions under the policy are expected to contribute 40% of the CAP EU funds to the achievement of the climate-related objectives.

The CAP can also provide the right support for on-farm or collective investments in energy efficiency and in the production of renewable energy, biogas installations and for advice and innovations in this field. Also, other tools and support instruments exist for energy efficiency and renewable energy production, at EU (e.g. Cohesion Policy, Recovery and Resilience Facility) but also at national level.

Measures in the Recovery and Resilience plans (RRPs) include research on climate technologies for agriculture, support for organic farming, modernising farming infrastructure and equipment and many measures helping the green transition of farmers. REPowerEU measures address the impact of increased energy prices and limit the risk of future negative impact of high energy prices.

The REPowerEU chapters in the RRPs have committed EUR 54.4 billion so far for measures to help citizens, including farmers, lower their energy bills taking into account the needs of the agricultural sector.
